nature-pol-203.title: Rio Principle 15: the precautionary approach
nature-pol-203.text: Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration says that where serious or irreversible damage threatens, lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone cost-effective preventive measures. This precautionary approach is a softer form of the {{ref:nature-pol-201}}, one that takes local capabilities and costs into account. Even the label is contested. The United States has opposed the word 'principle' in negotiations, because a principle of law is a source of law. The line between the two terms is described as diffuse and sometimes controversial. The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety builds on the approach of Principle 15.

nature-pol-202.title: Strong and weak precaution
nature-pol-202.text: Buying a smoke detector or wearing a seatbelt is weak precaution, and people practice it daily. Weak versions of the precautionary principle only permit action without full proof. They allow benefits to be weighed against costs, and economic factors may justify delay. Strong precaution requires regulation whenever harm is possible, even if the evidence is speculative and the economic costs are high. This 'no-regrets' stance ignores cost. The 1982 UN World Charter for Nature gave the strong version its first international recognition.

nature-pol-204.title: The precautionary dilemma: trivial or incoherent?
nature-pol-204.text: A common objection says the precautionary principle is caught in a trap: its weak versions are trivial and its strong versions incoherent. Cass Sunstein argued that the weak version only states a truism. Strong precaution, meanwhile, can itself cause harm, by blocking innovation and keeping current harmful technologies in use. Banning nuclear plants over low-probability risks, for example, means continued reliance on fossil-fuel plants and their air-pollution deaths. Critics conclude that no version is both useful and coherent. Its defenders reject that view.

nature-pol-230.title: Plan, Do, Check, Act: the cycle behind ISO 14001
nature-pol-230.text: ISO 14001 environmental management rests on a four-step cycle: Plan, Do, Check and Act. Planning starts with a review of how the organization's operations interact with the environment, its 'environmental aspects'. In the Check stage, performance is measured against targets and internal audits are held. A management review then resets the targets. Each turn of the cycle feeds a process of continual improvement.

nature-pol-185.title: Who writes the rules: consensus standards and private ones
nature-pol-185.text: Sustainability standards fall into two groups. Voluntary consensus standards come out of an agreed process, as at the International Organization for Standardization. Private standards are written by individual companies for themselves, such as Starbucks' C.A.F.E. Practices and Nespresso AAA. Some standards were launched by coalitions of firms, NGOs and development agencies to harmonize the rules. The Marine Stewardship Council standard is one.

nature-pol-190.title: The ecolabeling cycle: how labels spur green innovation
nature-pol-190.text: Ecolabeling is a repeating process, not a one-off stamp. Consumers, firms, governments and institutions interact through ecolabels, and the result is eco-innovation. Labeling encourages new green products and improves firms' environmental management strategy. Each turn of the cycle serves every party: consumers' expectations are met, firms gain value, and governments foster cleaner production and consumption.

nature-pol-189.title: Ecolabels as regulation without the state
nature-pol-189.text: At the 1992 Earth Summit, countries agreed to bring environmental issues into manufacturing and to steer consumption toward sustainable development. Ecolabeling fits that aim. It is a self-regulating, market-based tool that partly takes over from government {{ref:nature-pol-147}}. The standards are voluntary, but they put market pressure on large companies to adopt greener production. In this way ecolabeling has become a form of non-state authority, at national and international levels.

nature-pol-188.title: Can ecolabels become trade barriers?
nature-pol-188.text: Labels meant to help the planet can also hinder trade. To qualify for a foreign ecolabel, exporters must adjust to each market's production standards, which can cost money, information and expertise. Labeling programs often reflect the importing country's priorities and technologies, and may not fit the exporting country's environment. Hence the concern that ecolabels create obstacles to trade other than tariffs, the taxes on imports. Since 1995 the agreements of the {{ref:nature-pol-007}} have covered the possible effects of voluntary product standards and labels.

nature-pol-191.title: Energy labels: efficiency at a glance
nature-pol-191.text: The yellow US EnergyGuide label estimates an appliance's energy use, compares it with similar products and lists rough yearly running costs. It is an energy label: a label on a consumer appliance showing whether it uses energy efficiently compared with similar products. Canadian law requires the EnerGuide label on every new electrical appliance made in or imported into Canada. These labels show the energy used in operation. Energy input labeling, by contrast, shows the energy used to make the product.

nature-pol-217.title: Energy Star: a small budget, a big claimed payoff
nature-pol-217.text: Supporters of Energy Star cited estimated yearly energy cost savings of more than $40 billion, against about $32 million in yearly EPA funding. The US Environmental Protection Agency set up this voluntary labeling program in 1992, first for computers and displays. It now covers more than 75 product categories, plus homes, commercial buildings and industrial plants. Before 2011, products qualified on manufacturers' own data, which auditors found open to fraud. Since then independent labs and certifiers must test them. The label shows a product beats minimum guidelines, but it is not always the most efficient option available.

nature-pol-187.title: Three types of environmental label
nature-pol-187.text: The International Organization for Standardization sorts environmental labels into three types, by what they cover and how strictly they are checked. Type I (ISO 14024) is a voluntary label based on many criteria, checked by an independent third party that looks at a product's life cycle impacts. Type II (ISO 14021) is a claim a manufacturer or retailer makes about itself, without third-party auditing. Type III (ISO/TR 14025) declares measured life cycle data; it does not rate the product but helps buyers compare. 'Type I-like' labels cover a single issue, such as a pass/fail energy limit for appliances.

nature-pol-223.title: Does fair trade help the farmers?
nature-pol-223.text: One estimate found US exporters received only 2% of a US$5 per pound retail premium on coffee. Little of the extra price, in other words, may reach farmers. Studies disagree on whether fair trade raises producers' incomes and working conditions or mostly benefits intermediaries. A 2015 study found producer benefits close to zero, because of an oversupply of certification. Economists add a market argument. Coffee demand is highly inelastic, barely responding to price ({{ref:nature-econ-358}}), so more fair trade output can push down prices for the many non-certified farmers. Yet a study in the Journal of Economic Perspectives found fair trade meets many of its goals, though on a modest scale.

nature-pol-222.title: The fair trade premium: money for the community
nature-pol-222.text: In 2011 Fairtrade International's system paid €65 million in premiums to producers for community development. This social premium is extra money that buyers of fair trade goods pay to producer groups, which decide democratically how to spend it. Under Fairtrade it goes to the cooperative rather than directly to individual producers. Groups often spend it on public goods that government fails to provide, such as environmental projects, schools and water projects.

nature-pol-193.title: Energy subsidies: the case for and against
nature-pol-193.text: Should governments support energy prices or producers? Supporters say subsidies secure domestic supply, cut air pollution, help meet climate pledges, widen access to energy for the poor and protect jobs. Critics say fossil fuel subsidies raise consumption and waste, burden public finances and hold back cleaner technologies. They also miss the poor: in developing countries, most of the benefit goes to the richest 20% of households. The World Bank found subsidies to large energy companies unjustified, but saw a case for helping the poorest households get modern energy. Reform is hard, since many see it as governments taking something away.

nature-pol-235.title: Green public procurement: governments buying green
nature-pol-235.text: Rules can steer public bodies to buy efficient computers, recycled paper, electric vehicles and renewable energy. That is green public procurement, the part of sustainable public procurement that uses government buying power to reach environmental goals. It aims to cut greenhouse gas emissions, improve resource efficiency and grow the market for greener products, which can drive green innovation. It relies heavily on life cycle costing, which counts transport, installation, training, insurance and running costs as well as the purchase price.

nature-pol-196.title: Making electronics makers pay for e-waste
nature-pol-196.text: E-waste, used electronic equipment that cannot safely go out with household trash, contains lead, mercury, brominated flame-retardants and cadmium. All are dangerous to health and the environment. Producer responsibility rules tackle it by making producers pay for its {{ref:nature-eecon-038}}. That may lead them to design less toxic, longer-lasting electronics, so EPR is cited as a tool against planned obsolescence, products built to wear out early. Critics worry it could raise prices, slow innovation, or let manufacturers shred second-hand goods instead of reusing them. Whether it really speeds greener design is disputed.

nature-pol-195.title: Take-back programs: returning products to their makers
nature-pol-195.text: The earliest take-back schemes began in Europe, driven by scarce landfill space and hazardous parts. These waste policies require manufacturers to take back their products at the end of their useful life, or to help pay for collection and reprocessing. They were adopted where collection of hazardous products was lacking or too costly for local governments. The aims are to encourage designs that can be reused or remade, to put waste costs into product prices and to promote innovation in reprocessing.

nature-pol-216.title: The CAP's second pillar: money for the countryside
nature-pol-216.text: Since 2000 the EU farm policy has had a second pillar, which funds the economic, social and environmental development of the countryside. It works through seven-year rural development programs, of which there are 118 in the EU. One of its three axes supports land management that improves the environment and helps fight climate change. Projects can include protecting water quality, sustainable land management and planting trees against erosion and floods.

nature-pol-214.title: Paying farmers for conditions, not crops
nature-pol-214.text: On 26 June 2003 the EU reformed its farm support. It cut the link between subsidies and particular crops, and tied payments to environmental and other conditions. Under cross compliance, farmers who fail the strict environmental requirements face cuts in their subsidies. The aim was to free more money for environmental quality and animal welfare programs. In England, the Single Payment Scheme paid a flat rate of around £230 per hectare for keeping land fit for cultivation.

nature-pol-215.title: Hedgerows and birds: the farm policy's environmental record
nature-pol-215.text: Between 1980 and 2009 the farmland bird population fell from 600 million to 300 million, a loss of 50%. Critics blame EU farm subsidies, which drove a large expansion of production using fertilizers and pesticides. Removing hedgerows and plowing meadows made farming more efficient but cut farmland bird habitat. Reforms since 2004 claim to put the environment at the center of farm policy. In 2010 the EU said 31% of €5 billion for new agricultural challenges would go to protecting biodiversity in the countryside. Yet in 2024 the European Court of Auditors warned the policy was not aligned with the EU's Green Deal climate goals.

nature-pol-238.title: Voluntary agreements: environmental action by deal, not decree
nature-pol-238.text: Since the 1980s many governments have turned from regulation toward 'new' instruments, notably market instruments and voluntary agreements. In a voluntary environmental agreement, firms or other actors agree, without being forced, to take environmental action, often in a deal with government. This differs from command-and-control rules, where authorities dictate the performance or technology required ({{ref:nature-pol-147}}). In industrial countries, such agreements let companies gain recognition for going beyond minimum regulatory standards. In developing countries such as in Latin America, they are more often used to fix widespread non-compliance with mandatory rules. Some do not last. The EU first tackled car CO2 emissions through a voluntary agreement, and later replaced it with mandatory limits for new cars.

nature-pol-225.title: Grid parity: when clean power matches the grid price
nature-pol-225.text: Grid parity is the point at which electricity from an alternative technology costs the same as the average grid electricity price in an area. It is a moving target: parity can vary over the day, over years and from place to place. In some areas wind, landfill gas and biomass power are already cheaper than grid electricity. Parity has been reached in areas that use feed-in tariffs.

nature-pol-210.title: Carbon labels: the emissions behind a product
nature-pol-210.text: In 2006 the Carbon Trust introduced the first carbon label in the UK, the Carbon Reduction Label. A carbon emission label states the carbon dioxide emitted in making, transporting or disposing of a consumer product, its {{ref:nature-acct-031}}. Such labels focus on greenhouse gas emissions rather than direct energy use. The Carbon Trust label came with a condition: companies had to commit to cutting the product's embodied carbon or lose the label. The Swiss climatop label works differently. It marks products at least 20% better than others in their category.

nature-pol-236.title: Sustainable seafood guides and labels
nature-pol-236.text: Seafood advisory lists and certification schemes aim to make seafood supply chains transparent and to help shoppers choose seafood from well-managed stocks. The Marine Stewardship Council, for instance, runs a certification program for consumer seafood products. The economic impact of these schemes is unclear, but they bring non-monetary gains such as better reputation and reorganized supply chains. Their spread has a cost. Many conservationists feel the growing number of seafood labels is confusing consumers.

nature-pol-212.title: Chain of custody: tracking certified wood to the shop
nature-pol-212.text: Between January 2009 and May 2010, PEFC and FSC chain-of-custody certificates rose 88% to 23,717 worldwide. Chain-of-custody certification tracks certified material through every stage of processing and distribution, from the forest to the consumer. It keeps certified material identified or separate from non-certified material during manufacture. That provides evidence that certified material in a product really comes from certified forests.

nature-pol-219.title: What environmental certification cannot do
nature-pol-219.text: Usually only the best-performing operators get certified, so firms with no interest in environmental management stay outside. That is the first limit of voluntary certification. The second is cost. Suppliers usually bear it, and the extra profit often does not cover it. Many certification costs are fixed, so large producers gain an advantage over small ones through economies of scale. The third is reach. Tropical deforestation usually comes from converting forest to other uses, which lies outside forest management certification.

nature-pol-228.title: Local content rules: buy local to qualify
nature-pol-228.text: Ontario's 2009 Green Energy and Green Economy Act made wind and solar farms use Ontario-made parts to qualify for subsidies. That is a local content requirement: a rule requiring producers to source a minimum share of goods, labor or services locally. The Ontario law created many jobs, cut emissions and greatly expanded the province's renewable energy industry.

nature-pol-227.title: Picking winners: the risks of green industrial policy
nature-pol-227.text: Can governments pick the right firms and industries? Proponents and skeptics of green industrial policy agree there are risks, but disagree on whether governments can choose well enough to justify it. Subsidies are especially prone to {{ref:nature-pol-042}}, because special interests press to keep them even when they are no longer needed. Support also invites {{ref:nature-pol-040}}, and policy may end up driven by political rather than economic concerns. Some failures are inevitable. Governments can reduce the risk by testing policies in parts of the country first.

reviews.subsidies-information-and-voluntary-appr: Besides taxes and caps, governments steer the economy by paying, informing and persuading. Subsidies pass money to favored activities, but fossil fuel, fishing and farm subsidies show how support can turn perverse, harming budgets and the environment at once. Information tools, from ecolabels and energy labels to pollution registers, let shoppers and neighbors judge for themselves. Voluntary standards, certification and agreements let firms go beyond the rules, though usually only the best performers take part. Beneath many of these tools lies the precautionary principle, the case for caution when science is incomplete, which remains as contested as the tools themselves.
